extracted.intended_audience: corporate executives, IP managers, patent professionals, and policymakers concerned with NPE litigation and defensive patent strategies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for evaluating and operating defensive patent-aggregation approaches (e.g., RPX, AST) and for assessing patent litigation risk from NPEs. Focuses on when to buy/license patents, indicators of litigation risk, and measures of success for defensive programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of claim charts / reputable broker indicates litigation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: "So, for example, when we look at a reputable patent broker who’s got a track record of selling to NPEs ... if that guy has a patent and it’s a decent patent and it’s got claim charts, an NPE’s going to buy it. It’s a litigation waiting to happen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim charts in offering materials map patent claims to accused products and identify likely targets. A broker with a history of selling to NPEs plus claim charts is a strong signal the portfolio will be acquired by an NPE and generate litigation; treat such offerings as high-priority for defensive acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate patents by probabilities, statistics, and transaction costs
rubrics_metrics.description: "What counts today are probabilities, statistics, and, most of all, transaction costs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat patents as absolute, deterministic rights. Assess expected value using probabilities of validity/infringement, likely settlement amounts, defense costs, and transaction costs (e.g., forum advantages). Use statistical estimates (e.g., roughly half of patents tossed when tested in court) when valuing risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemptive purchase of dangerous patents is most efficient
rubrics_metrics.description: RPX’s strategy: buy problematic patents before litigation begins because this usually costs far less than the combined settlements and legal fees defendants would otherwise incur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare acquisition price vs expected aggregate costs of litigation/settlement (example: a $2.5M portfolio later produced $78M in defendant costs). Prioritize pre-litigation purchases where expected savings exceed purchase and membership costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a valuation algorithm to decide buy vs license/options
rubrics_metrics.description: RPX uses a valuation algorithm to decide whether to buy entire portfolios or only license rights/options for subsets of clients when full purchase cannot be justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many defendants are involved, buying the whole portfolio may be uneconomic; instead buy licensing rights or options for subscribing members and negotiate buyouts for others. The algorithm should incorporate defendant count, member coverage, expected defense costs, and resale/liquidation value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription-based pooling of funds to increase buying power
rubrics_metrics.description: RPX members pay annual subscription fees (ranging from about $85,000 to as much as $7 million or more per year, depending on net operating income) to fund purchases and negotiations on behalf of members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A predictable subscription model aligns incentives, aggregates capital to compete in the secondary market, and can reduce member exposure; measure potential pooled budget vs market prices to estimate achievable risk reduction (RPX suggests 85–90% reduction with larger pools).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pledge to never assert patents enhances defensive credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: RPX has spent more than $500 million purchasing rights to patents which it pledges never to assert against anyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal, enforceable non-assertion policy (or structural design preventing assertion) is central to differentiate a defensive aggregator from an NPE; this pledge is a trust-and-marketing criterion for attracting members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-and-release / divestiture is controversial
rubrics_metrics.description: RPX sometimes sells patents — after licensing them to all its members — back into the open market, including to NPEs (a practice similar to AST’s 'catch and release').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divestiture can recycle capital to buy more patents but risks being perceived as indistinguishable from trolls if resale enables future assertion. Use transparency with members and clear governance rules to mitigate reputational and policy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust / monopsony risk for defensive aggregators
rubrics_metrics.description: An NPE (Cascades) brought an antitrust suit accusing RPX of acting as a monopsonist — a buyers’ monopoly — that collusively drives down the value of settlements to which NPEs are entitled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design aggregation practices to avoid coordinated behavior that could invite antitrust claims: document independent valuations, avoid price-fixing communications, and maintain legal counsel on competitive risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum-shopping and venue concentration as a red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Many NPE suits concentrate in favorable plaintiffs’ venues (40% of NPE defendants last year were sued in the Eastern District of Texas), suggesting forum-shopping and increased nuisance settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing litigation risk, account for venue-specific plaintiff advantages that increase settlement probabilities and costs; factor likely forum into expected-value models and settlement strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent quality: 'little-step improvements' can still create significant risk
rubrics_metrics.description: "Most patents involve 'little-step improvements,' not breakthroughs, which are nevertheless patentable... The intractable problems stem from 'shades of gray.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore patents that seem incremental; their uncertain scope and borderline validity can produce costly disputes. Valuation models should capture 'gray area' patents' asymmetric litigation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation cost composition: attorneys take majority share
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: a portfolio asking $2.5M later produced $20M in settlements and $58M in defense fees; 74% of the $78M aggregate went to defense attorneys and plaintiffs’ counsel likely got ~30% of settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing acquisition vs litigation, include attorney fees, contingency fees, and settlement splits. High legal-cost ratios strengthen the case for preemptive purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use data-driven decision-making and shared member cost data
rubrics_metrics.description: "Look at the data. Look at the patterns. Quantify your decisions." RPX leverages digitized court dockets and confidential client cost data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain databases of dockets, asserted claims, past settlements, defense spend, and broker behavior. Use empirical patterns to prioritize purchases and set subscription pricing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: recruit members before suits; recruitment post-suit is easier but costlier
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, it’s easier to recruit clients when they have already been sued. By then, however, the patent has usually become too expensive for RPX to buy anymore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively market defensive coverage and monitor market offerings to sign members pre-litigation; balance sales realism (clients sign when under pressure) against economics of late entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buying licensing rights/options to assemble settlements and induce join-ins
rubrics_metrics.description: When RPX cannot justify buying the whole patent for all defendants, it buys the licensing rights for its clients and options for others, then offers buyouts to remaining defendants to induce them to join RPX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partial rights and options strategically to leverage member concentration in multi-defendant suits. Structure options to be attractive to holdouts while preserving overall economic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design defensive consortia to structurally prevent assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Allied Security Trust (AST) uses 'catch and release' and licenses won patents to bidding members then sells them back into the market — guaranteeing AST can never itself become a troll because it retains no patents to sue upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consortia can adopt governance rules (e.g., no retention of enforceable assertion rights) to reduce reputational and legal risk of becoming an NPE; document lifecycle of acquired patents and member rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat patents as bargaining chips rather than definitive titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Robin Feldman: 'A patent does not grant a definitive set of rights... Rather, it is an invitation to bargain over the definition of those rights.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame patent strategy around negotiation leverage and expected settlements rather than absolute legal entitlements; plan for bargaining dynamics, counterclaims, and invalidity challenges as part of value assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure success by dismissals, suits averted, and cost savings
rubrics_metrics.description: RPX reports metrics: spent >$500M, bought >3,800 patents, bought clients 430 dismissals from 60 litigations, and claims to have averted >2,000 suits; these are used as success indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track concrete outcomes (dismissals, reduced defendant counts, suits averted, aggregate legal spend saved) to evaluate defensive program ROI and to justify membership pricing.
